title: Neptune's Moons Might Be Leftovers from a Giant Crash!
summary:
Imagine a giant game of cosmic bumper cars. That's what might have happened around Neptune billions of years ago! Scientists think that Neptune's biggest moon, Triton, crashed into other moons and smashed them into pieces. Then those pieces came back together to form the moons we see today.

How do they know? They used the James Webb Space Telescope to look at three of Neptune's small moons: Larissa, Galatea, and Proteus. They found clay minerals on them — and that's a big surprise!

Why? Because clay minerals need a lot of heat to form. That heat could only come from inside a large icy body. So, the clay might be from the inside of an ancient moon that got turned inside out by the crash.

Study lead author Ryleigh Davis said, "The most surprising thing is simply that we found clay minerals at all."

Triton is special because it orbits Neptune backwards — opposite to the way Neptune spins. That's weird! Most big moons go the same way as their planet spins. This makes scientists think Triton was captured by Neptune's gravity from far away. When it arrived, it might have acted like a wrecking ball, smashing Neptune's original moons.

So, the next time you look at the night sky, remember: some moons might be made of pieces of other moons that crashed together long ago. Space is full of surprises!
why_it_matters: Learning about collisions around Neptune helps us understand how moons and planets form everywhere, including our own moon—one day, space discoveries like these might even teach us about the history of Earth.

background_read: Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun, and it has 16 moons, many of which are tiny and icy.
Triton is its largest moon and is weird because it orbits in the opposite direction that Neptune spins—this is very rare for a large moon.
Scientists think Triton was captured by Neptune's gravity long ago, maybe from the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy objects beyond the planets.
The James Webb Space Telescope (the biggest space telescope ever, launched in 2021) can look at these faraway moons in amazing detail and help solve their mysteries.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists using the James Webb Space Telescope
WHAT: Found clay minerals on small moons, giving clues that Triton crashed into and destroyed earlier moons
WHERE: Around Neptune, in the outer part of our solar system
WHY: To explain why the moons look the way they do and why Triton's orbit is so unusual

perspectives.description: This discovery is thrilling because it reveals a dramatic, violent history that created the moons we see today, showing that the outer solar system was far from boring.
Some scientists caution that the idea of a giant crash is still just a theory, and more observations are needed to be completely sure it happened.
Understanding how moons are built from smashed-up pieces helps astronomers piece together the story of our solar system, which is full of surprises and still being written.
